Iron Fish Discovers Underlying Inflation Vulnerability and Announces Termination of Remaining Network Support On October 31, the privacy public chain Iron Fish announced that it would terminate all remaining support for its network. Several days prior, the team discovered abnormal activity involving the wIRON and ChainPort cross-chain bridge. A joint investigation confirmed that the root cause was an inflation vulnerability in the Iron Fish blockchain itself, not the cross-chain bridge. The vulnerability dates back to a Merkle tree implementation code commit in early 2019. It involves the calculation logic of the nullifier (an identifier used to prevent double-spending) in privacy tickets, allowing attackers to repeatedly spend the same ticket and transfer assets out via the ChainPort cross-chain bridge. The team stated that the relevant code had previously been included in internal and external audits, but the vulnerability went undetected. Iron Fish has submitted a patch and included a detailed recap in the relevant PR; the team will subsequently close and archive the code repository. On October 31st, according to The Defiant, developer nicolashw submitted a draft Ethereum core improvement proposal on October 30th, proposing to allow external accounts (EOAs) to permanently disable EIP-7702 delegation functionality while retaining existing addresses, normal transfers, and contract call capabilities. Unlike simply clearing the current delegation, this operation is irreversible, preventing the account from authorizing smart contract code to run on its behalf again in the future. However, this mechanism cannot prevent fund transfers after a private key leak, nor will it revoke existing token authorizations, and may also affect account recovery and asset access that rely on delegation functionality. Currently, this draft has not been merged and has not received an official EIP number; if adopted later, it will still need to be activated through an Ethereum network upgrade. Cryptocurrency ▌21Shares: Bitcoin only fell about 2% after the Binance hack, far less than the 26% drop after the FTX incident. On October 31, 21Shares released an analysis report on the Binance hack, stating that Binance suffered an attack of approximately $6.3 billion on October 29, and approximately $3 billion of stolen assets have been frozen. Binance has pledged to bear all losses. Within 24 hours of the incident, Bitcoin fell slightly by over 2%, significantly less than the approximately 26% drop following the FTX incident in November 2022. 21Shares emphasized that this incident was a security vulnerability specific to Binance, and the Bitcoin network itself was not attacked. The report indicates that Binance stated it will cover all losses through the SAFU Fund and company funds. Based on a Bitcoin price of approximately $78,509, the 15,000 BTC held by the SAFU Fund are worth approximately $1.18 billion, covering about 36% of the loss of unfrozen assets; the remainder will be covered by company funds.

▌AI Agent Project Recall Shuts Down, Plans to Burn 35.86% of Tokens

On October 31st, according to an announcement from the Recall Foundation, the board of directors of the decentralized AI agent evaluation network Recall announced the shutdown of the foundation, stating that after evaluating protocol adoption rates, operating costs, and growth prospects, continued development was not commercially viable. This decision was unrelated to hacking or security incidents. The foundation plans to burn approximately 358.6 million RECALL tokens under its control, representing approximately 35.86% of the total supply. Token holders will not receive any allocation, redemption, or buyback; the remaining approximately $3.7 million will be used to repay creditors and cover liquidation costs. The official application will become read-only from November 30th, with liquidation expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027. Stakinged RECALL tokens are not included in the burning; holders can unstake them themselves, and new applications will no longer have a 30-day cooling-off period.

On October 31, the Solana ecosystem lending protocol Jupiter Lend announced that the liquidity shortage on Jupiter Lend has ended. With liquidity replenished, USDC withdrawals have returned to normal, and the previously surged fund utilization rate has also subsided.

Anthropic PBC pledged in its IPO filing that, as infrastructure expands rapidly, the company will spend nearly $900 billion through future obligations on servers, buildings, and electricity. This amount far exceeds the liabilities listed on its balance sheet that investors can directly see.

Investors need to delve into the notes to Anthropic's financial statements to see the details of its planned expenditures—these off-balance-sheet obligations include future lease contracts and procurement agreements for data centers, power, and GPUs. David Trainer, CEO of investment research firm New Constructs, stated that Anthropic's committed expenditures, often referred to as "hidden debt," are substantial. He stated, "They have to invest heavily in training, reasoning, and energy." (Bloomberg) ▌ US Treasury yields generally fell by more than 30 basis points in October. Russian Presidential Aide Ushakov stated on the same day that Ukraine had once again ignored US President Trump's call to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, and that Trump's stance on the issue was firm but Ukraine had not complied. data.title: Anthropic is about to go public: Is large-scale modeling a good business?
data.description:
On October 26, 2026, Anthropic officially filed for an IPO with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, planning to list on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Media reports projected a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Even before the bell rang, its value was already at least a trillion dollars. Regardless of its post-IPO performance, this day is likely to leave a mark on economic history. Anthropic is a significant bellwether in this intelligent revolution. Many people link the economic value of AI with the commercial value of model companies: since AI can change the world, leading model companies should be making a fortune, right? If Anthropic continues its upward trajectory, the market will have even more reason to believe that today's massive investment will eventually pay off. The story grew grander, and more money was invested. But if growth fell short of expectations, doubts would spread along the industry chain: if model companies weren't making money, how long could orders from cloud vendors, chipmakers, and data centers continue? A single company's performance thus influenced confidence in the entire technological revolution. But this connection also easily obscured a difference: the wealth created by AI might remain with large model companies, or it might flow to businesses and consumers using it through lower prices and higher efficiency. Anthropic's IPO presented us with two questions simultaneously: How much value can the intelligent revolution create? And how much value can one share by investing in a large model company? The answers to these two questions are not necessarily the same. We often say, "Great industries, mediocre investments." If we were to rank the greatest industries of the 20th century, electricity would certainly be at the head of the table. Electricity has transformed factories, cities, and the lives of ordinary people. But just because lights illuminate countless homes doesn't mean that everyone who invests in electricity will benefit. Around 1900, there were hundreds of electricity companies in the United States, most of which later failed due to market competition, debt crises, and the Great Depression. Among them, one notable name was Insall. He initially served as Edison's personal secretary, taking over the Chicago Edison Company in 1892. Through large-scale generators, grid-connected power supply, and low-price expansion, he turned electricity into a massive business. However, in 1932, his company went bankrupt due to excessive debt, leaving 600,000 shareholders with nothing. He fled to Greece but was extradited back to the United States for trial. The automotive industry, hailed as the crown jewel of the industrial age, has seen investors in auto stocks consistently profit. Warren Buffett once said he possessed a 70-page list of over 2,000 American automakers from that era. Sadly, nearly a century later, only General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler remain, and their long-term returns have been less than satisfactory. From 1956 to 2019, Ford's annualized return was 5.6%, which, if you bought into the leading company, was roughly equivalent to buying government bonds. General Motors even went into bankruptcy reorganization in 2009. Later, car production continued, but the old company's common stock was officially cancelled on March 31, 2011, with shareholders receiving no compensation. Changing the world and making shareholders money are two different things. Buffett's conclusion is: the key to investing is not judging the extent to which an industry will change society, but judging a company's competitive advantage and how long that advantage can be maintained. Reading Anthropic's prospectus, I always thought of these stories. "Intelligence will change the world" easily leads to the conclusion that "large-scale companies will make investors a lot of money." But there's a long way to go from the former to the latter. If we look at Buffett's stock-picking preferences, it can be summarized in one sentence: profits can grow continuously without requiring a proportional increase in new capital. His example is See's Candies. From its acquisition in 1972 to 2007, See's generated $1.35 billion in pre-tax profits, while only needing to invest an additional $32 million in operating capital to support business growth. The remaining money could be given to the parent company, paid taxes, and then reinvested in other businesses. Using this standard to measure Anthropic is clearly not suitable at present. However, it's not surprising that a rapidly expanding company at the forefront of technology would experience cash flow difficulties. The key question is: going forward, is it possible for it to become a business that consistently generates cash flow for shareholders? We can break this down into three parts: First, can training large models generate revenue? Second, how much more money needs to be invested annually to continue selling AI? Third, can the profits remain with the model company long-term? Three Questions About the Business Model of Large Models

First, can training large models make money?

First, can training large models be profitable?

Anthropic's business is quite simple: selling "intelligence" by token. Of its $16.286 billion revenue in the first half of 2026, approximately $13.1 billion (80%) came from usage-based billing; subscriptions such as Enterprise Edition and Pro/Max generated $3.2 billion (20%). Eighty percent is charged based on usage, and the remaining 20% ​​is charged via monthly or annual fees. This resembles a power company's bill, rather than a software or platform company's bill.

This business model has one advantage: once the same model is trained, serving the first customer and the 100 millionth customer doesn't require retraining. Inference still consumes computing power, but the initial R&D investment can be amortized by increased usage. As long as the increase in usage is enough to offset the price reduction, revenue can continue to grow; if the unit service cost decreases faster than the price, the gross margin will also increase. Anthropic's financial statements already show this change. Operating revenue increased from $41 million in 2023 to $386 million in 2024, and then jumped to $4.585 billion in 2025. By 2026, it had achieved $16.286 billion in revenue in the first half of the year alone. Since 2024, while revenue has expanded, gross margin has also improved rapidly: from -94.8% in 2024 to 39.5% in 2025, and further to 85.4% in the first half of 2026. In other words, for every $100 a customer paid in 2024, the company's corresponding operating cost was close to $195; by the first half of 2026, this cost had dropped to about $15. Compared to major Chinese model manufacturers, this figure is quite impressive. Zhipu and MiniMax's revenue is less than 1% of Anthropic's, and their gross profit margin is only around 20%. At least in terms of serving paying customers, Anthropic has crossed a significant threshold: customer payments significantly exceed current operating costs. However, a high gross profit margin does not necessarily mean the company is profitable. Large models are divided into training and inference phases. The $2.38 billion in operating costs mainly corresponds to the computing power and infrastructure used to serve customers during the inference phase of the trained models. The money spent on continuing to research and train the next generation of models is primarily recorded in R&D expenses and hasn't been deducted from the $85 gross profit. This leads to the second question—how much more money needs to be invested each year to continue selling intelligence? See's Candy doesn't require technological advancements; it doesn't need to invent a chocolate bar with twice the intelligence every year. Leading-edge model companies don't have that luxury. Customers buy Claude largely because of its capabilities. But competitors are constantly releasing new models, and customers' demands for accuracy, speed, price, and task completion are constantly increasing. The company must continue to invest to secure the foundation for the next round of revenue. How long can a cutting-edge model stay ahead? Currently, it seems to be only a few months. A telling figure in the prospectus is that from July to September 2026, over 80% of Anthropic's revenue came from model versions released between April and September of that year. The main driver of revenue is now the models released in the last six months. Previously, power plants were built, depreciated over 30-40 years, and then generated electricity revenue for decades. Now, large model companies rebuild an even larger power plant every year. The prospectus shows that in the first half of 2026, total computing power and infrastructure costs amounted to $8.945 billion. Of the 2.38 billion yuan recorded in operating costs and used to serve customers, only 6 billion yuan was used to train the next generation of models. In other words, for every 100 yuan spent on computing power, less than 30 yuan was used to sell tokens, and over 70 yuan was used to build the next model. Of course, continuous investment itself is not a sin. Buffett also invests in utilities that require substantial capital. The real dividing line is: does each additional investment yield a commensurate return? If R&D investment can open up a larger market, increase customer payments, and reduce service costs, then this money is a valuable investment. If the investment is increasing but mainly used to avoid being left behind by competitors, shareholders must ask: Is the company accumulating advantages or simply paying the price left at the table? What's more complicated is that these investments are no longer just R&D budgets that can be adjusted annually. Anthropic doesn't build its own data centers; its computing power is mainly leased from Amazon and Google. Therefore, its balance sheet doesn't show much factory or equipment; "capital expenditures" are hidden in operating costs and off-balance-sheet procurement commitments—in the first half of 2026, Anthropic's non-cancellable procurement commitments increased from approximately $54.6 billion at the end of 2025 to $265.6 billion at the end of June, a 4.9-fold increase in six months; projected lease payments for contracts signed but not yet leased increased from $50.2 billion to $321.4 billion. Subsequently, the company signed or revised a large number of infrastructure agreements. If subsequent commitments and conditional expenditures are included, the future expenditures involved reach trillions of dollars. These so-called non-cancellable procurement commitments, though not appearing on the balance sheet, are essentially a form of liability. For example, in Anthropic's agreements with Google and Amazon, as long as the supplier fulfills its obligations, the company is usually required to make up the agreed minimum expenditure even if the actual usage is insufficient. This creates a "short-term borrowing for long-term investment" type of maturity mismatch: the company promises suppliers fixed expenditures for many years, while customers promise monthly, fixed-amount revenue that can be discontinued at any time. Of the $13.1 billion in revenue generated in the first half of the year, not a single penny came from customer contracts with five-year terms. In the history of electricity, Insall failed precisely because of this. His power plants were built on debt, and electricity bills were collected monthly; after 1929, the Great Depression caused a sharp decline in electricity consumption, but the debt did not shrink accordingly. Technology creates value, but it doesn't guarantee that shareholders will live to see that value realized. The third question: Can the profits remain with the model company long-term? This is a matter of competitive advantage. Why do customers choose Claude? Because it's easy to use. But what if another company is equally good, and cheaper? If customers only access large models via APIs, they can easily switch vendors. If competitors release models with better performance, customers will switch. For example, in September 2026, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra. The following week, on the third-party model platform OpenRouter, users spent more money on OpenAI models than on Anthropic. Relying solely on temporary technological advantages, the large model business can easily become a commodity. For example, electricity is a commodity; various power plants produce electricity of similar quality and price. Few people question which power plant produced this particular kilowatt-hour. A true competitive advantage comes only from deep integration with customers. Another detail in the prospectus: Anthropic acknowledges that bottlenecks in enterprise deployment are not only model capabilities, but also inadequate system connectivity, lack of established governance rules, and redesigned workflows. Therefore, the company sends dedicated teams to client organizations to help design and deploy specific applications. The Anthropic prospectus mentions AIG, a large insurance company. AIG's collaboration with Anthropic involves embedding Claude into the underwriting process to jointly build business applications. Previously, underwriters might spend weeks collecting data before starting to compile risk summaries. Now, in already deployed businesses, they can start working from the risk summaries and complete audit trails generated by Claude, focusing their efforts on review and judgment. According to the company, AIG Assist has reduced application review time by more than 90% in its deployed business scope. At this point, customers are not just buying a model response, but also integrating data, revising governance rules, and redeploying employees. When these processes heavily rely on Claude, switching vendors becomes more difficult. However, the moat formed by deep customer ties may not belong to the model company, but also to the application company building on top of the model. For example, WorkBuddy's approach keeps the underlying model replaceable, keeping customers' work on a single platform. The domestic version currently lists built-in models including Hunyuan, DeepSeek, Zhipu, MiniMax, and Kimi, and users can also integrate their purchased third-party model services. The advantage of this is that WorkBuddy can integrate regardless of which model prevails. The model handles understanding and reasoning, while the workbench organizes tools and execution processes. Workbuddy also integrates with WeChat Work, so employees don't need to change their daily work interface; AI can directly participate in the team's collaborative processes of task assignment, deliverables, and review and modification. As a team's data, tool connections, work standards, and collaboration habits gradually converge here, changing the underlying model doesn't necessarily require changing the entire work environment. Competition among model vendors can actually become a condition for the workbench to improve services and control costs. If a customer relies on a specific model, the advantage may remain with the model company; if a customer relies on a workbench that organizes models, data, processes, and tools, the advantage may be concentrated in applications like WorkBuddy. So, is large-scale modeling a good business? Anthropic's prospectus offers a significant improvement over the previous notion that "models only burn money": direct service costs are covered by revenue, gross profit is rapidly improving, and operating cash flow is turning positive. However, it hasn't yet proven that it can reliably retain cash available to shareholders after continuously developing next-generation models and fulfilling its long-term computing power commitments. If I were to boldly predict the future, I believe the ultimate outcome of the large-scale modeling competition will likely see two types of businesses: basic intelligence will increasingly resemble a utility, while cutting-edge intelligence will become more like a "luxury." As technology advances, price competition will intensify as more and more models overcome the capability barriers of everyday tasks. Organizing meeting minutes, categorizing goods, writing a notification, identifying anomalies in spreadsheets—in the real world, much of the work requires accuracy, stability, and affordability, not just intelligence. To accomplish these tasks, there's no reason for companies to pay for the world's smartest model every time. When several models can perform the same task well, customers will naturally start comparing prices. At this point, basic intelligence will increasingly resemble services like water, electricity, and communication: readily available, purchased on demand, with suppliers competing on cost, scale, and service quality. Intelligence becoming infrastructure may mean it's more indispensable, but also harder to sell at a high price. Companies like Anthropic, which pursue "top-tier intelligence," can still be the "LV of the large-scale model world": in a market where basic capabilities are becoming increasingly widespread, they can retain a niche where customers are willing to pay more—continuously delivering better results on complex tasks. Finally, stepping outside the perspective of a single company or industry, from a long-term perspective, the road for AI is still very long. Even now, we are still in the early stages of the intelligent revolution. Anthropic's prospectus also reveals that AI penetration remains very low—while over half of Fortune 500 companies are Anthropic customers with annual spending exceeding $100,000, their average spending on Anthropic is less than 0.1% of their total expenditure, with even the top 10 users accounting for less than 1%. The Anthropic prospectus is also interesting; it doesn't begin with its own performance figures, but with three images: a red bacterial colony, a cross-section of an ammonite, and an ancient celestial map. What does this mean? I believe it represents the vast space waiting to be explored by humankind, from microscopic life to the macroscopic universe. The accompanying text reads: "We believe that AI is one of the most far-reaching technologies in human history. If managed properly, it can rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, significantly increase economic growth rates, make cures for major diseases readily available, and solve problems that have remained unsolved for generations." I also believe in such a vast and promising future. But the road to it is destined to be winding and arduous.

data.title: One fish, multiple uses – An analysis of the $780,000 theft from zkLink
data.description:
Background

On October 29, 2026, the well-known cross-chain protocol zkLink was attacked, resulting in a loss of approximately $783,000. The following is a detailed analysis of this attack by the SlowMist security team:

Prerequisite Knowledge

zkLink is a multi-chain zk rollup protocol.

function claimMessage( address _sourceChainCanonicalMessageService, bytes calldata _sourceChainClaimCallData, IL1Gateway _sourceChainL1Gateway, uint256 _receiveValue, bytes calldata _receiveCallData, bytes calldata _forwardParams) external payable nonReentrant onlyRelayer { assembly { tstore(claiming.slot, 1) } // Exploitation point 1: The Arbitrator, as itself, executes arbitrary calldata on any address specified by the relayer. Address.functionCall(_sourceChainCanonicalMessageService, _sourceChainClaimCallData); bytes32 _finalizeMessageHash; assembly { _finalizeMessageHash := tload(finalizeMessageHash.slot) } // Exploitation point 2: The comparison is transient storage The old value in the code does not require that the current call actually occurred. `receiveMessage require( _finalizeMessageHash == keccak256(abi.encode(_sourceChainL1Gateway, _receiveValue, _receiveCallData)), "Incorrect finalize data" ); // ... The message is then forwarded to the target gateway according to the branch.` The first exploit point is that the "external execution content" is entirely determined by the relayer. `_sourceChainCanonicalMessageService` and `_sourceChainClaimCallData` are parameters passed to the relayer, and the Arbitrator contract will call and execute them as itself. Normally, this is a claim interface for a source chain message service; however, when an attacker changes the target to a gateway registered in the Arbitrator contract, the actual execution can call the function in the gateway that has the `onlyArbitrator` decorator check. The second exploit point is that the "consistency check" is bypassed due to the characteristics of transient storage. The check reads the `finalizeMessageHash` from the transient storage, and this slot is never cleared within the same transaction, nor does it become invalid after a call ends. As long as a genuine claim occurs once within the same transaction and the slot is written, the subsequent `claimMessage` can reuse it to pass the check, even if the second call does not claim any message. The attacker only needs to make the (gateway, value, callData) declarations of the two calls completely identical. That is, the successful check proves that "a claim matching these declarations has occurred once within this transaction", not that "this call claimed this message". So why can the batch root used for withdrawals be forged? Because the Arbitrator contract, after directing the target to EthereumGateway via an external call, calls the `sendMessage` function: This function only checks if the caller is an Arbitrator contract, and then forwards the `callData` to the ZkLink contract. Since the call was indeed initiated by the Arbitrator contract, the check passes. The attacker fills _callData with syncBatchRoot(116409, fake root, 0):

function syncBatchRoot(uint256 _batchNumber, bytes32 _l2LogsRootHash, uint256 _forwardEthAmount) external payable onlyGateway { // Only check if the caller is a gateway, do not verify any batch proof require(msg.value == _forwardEthAmount, "Invalid forward amount"); if (_batchNumber > totalBatchesExecuted) { totalBatchesExecuted = _batchNumber; } l2LogsRootHashes[_batchNumber] = _l2LogsRootHash; // Directly overwrite the log root of this batch emit SyncBatchRoot(_batchNumber, The ZkLink contract's `onlyGateway` function requires the caller to be its own configured gateway, and the EthereumGateway contract forwarded this call, so the check passed. The attacker then used the next batch number, 116409 (which hadn't yet been executed), along with a self-constructed log root, to rewrite `l2LogsRootHashes[116409]` from zero to a forged value, and incidentally pushed `totalBatchesExecuted` from 116408 to 116409. With the root forged, the Merkle proof would pass, and the withdrawal message could therefore be arbitrarily constructed. Thus, withdrawals could be made using the forged proof. Attack Step Analysis

Attack Transaction: 0x4f3c23e75b9134e8cae5a462550daad42fbbc19242567fcc34c0a035e297462c

Attacker's EOA: 0xaca0655a11200a80d33d0e48786317304cde5718

2. The attacker first performs a genuine Linea cross-chain claim, calling Arbitrator.claimMessage through the SyncL2TxHashRelayer contract to submit a genuine Linea message proof, specifying the "source chain message service address" as Linea Rollup, and attaching a claimMessageWithProof proof. This message is a Linea→Ethereum cross-chain message sent by the attacker on Linea, with the recipient being LineaL1Gateway, and its content instructing it to forward a syncL2TxHash(_l2TxHash,_primaryChainL2TxHash) to the target gateway. After the Linea Rollup verification passes, it calls back to LineaL1Gateway, which in turn calls back to the Arbitrator contract's receiveMessage function, writing the hash of this message into the finalizeMessageHash of transient storage. The claimMessage function then compares this value. In other words, the attacker uses a genuine, harmless claim process to obtain the verification value finalizeMessageHash and keep it in the transaction. The SyncL2TxHashRelayer contract is registered as a relayer in the Arbitrator contract, and the claimPrimaryChainSyncL2TxHashMessage function has no access control; any address can use its identity to call the claimMessage function of the Arbitrator contract. Furthermore, the claimMessage function allows the relayer to specify the source chain message service address. In addition, the verification value written in this actual claim will remain in the transient storage of this transaction until the transaction is completed.

3. Next, the attacking contract calls the same relayer again, only changing two parameters: the source chain message service is changed from Linea Rollup to EthereumGateway registered by the Arbitrator contract itself, and _sourceChainClaimCallData is changed to sendMessage(0, syncBatchRoot(116409, 0x1934a1...a8, 0), ""). The remaining parameters—source gateway, received amount, declared received calldata, and forwarding parameters—are identical byte-by-byte to those in the previous step. These parameters are precisely the values ​​used to check `finalizeMessageHash`, because the value of `finalizeMessageHash` is stored in transient storage and is never cleared within the same transaction. It is not bound to whether the message has actually been claimed in this call. Furthermore, the target address and calldata of the external call are not checked, so the value left from the previous claim can be directly reused in the second call. `Address.functionCall` then allows the Arbitrator contract to execute the arbitrary call specified by the attacker in its own name. This is the core flaw of this attack. In other words, this call did not claim any message, but the check of the claimMessage function still passed, and the attacker's external call to the EthereumGateway contract's sendMessage function had already been executed before the check. 4. When the Arbitrator calls the EthereumGateway contract's sendMessage function, because calldata is exactly the syncBatchRoot(116409, forged root, 0) filled in by the attacker, ZkLink records the forged root as the log root of this batch. From the on-chain results, we can see that ZkLink issues a SyncBatchRoot(116409, 0x1934a1c3…) event. The stored l2LogsRootHashes[116409] changes from zero to the root constructed by the attacker, and totalBatchesExecuted also changes from 116408 to 116409. At this point, the forged root has "legally" entered the protocol ledger. Both calls forward a syncL2TxHash call, writing l2TxHashMap[0x2575…] to 0xe9ec…. This step itself is harmless; it's just a byproduct of reusing the checksum. Because EthereumGateway.sendMessage only verifies whether the caller is an Arbitrator contract, it forwards the calldata to ZkLink as is; ZkLink.syncBatchRoot also only verifies whether the caller is a gateway contract, without verifying any batch proof. Both layers of "recognizing only the caller, not the content" checks pass, allowing the forged root to be written as a legitimate root. 5. After the root is rewritten, as long as the withdrawal message can calculate a proof against this root, it can pass verification. The attacking contract continuously initiates 12 final withdrawal calls, all pointing to batch 116409: first an ETH withdrawal, followed by 11 ERC-20 withdrawals. Each message carries 4 Merkle nodes, which are constructed by the attacker according to their forged root, so the proof must be valid and pass. ETH withdrawals are processed directly by the ZkLink contract, while 11 ERC-20 withdrawals are processed by the L1ERC20Bridge. After the proof is passed, the tokens are directly transferred from the bridge contract to the attacker's EOA. Although both contracts record "This message has been withdrawn," this marker only prevents duplicate submissions and cannot identify that the message itself never occurred in L2. The withdrawal contract only verifies whether "this message is contained in the tree corresponding to the root of the stored batch," but does not verify whether the root itself comes from a real L2 execution. Once the root is forged, any message can be used to calculate a valid proof. The core problem of this attack is that arbitrary external calls to the Arbitrator contract, combined with uncleaned transient storage, can be directly reused for verification. On the one hand, `Arbitrator.claimMessage` allows the relayer to specify arbitrary targets and calldata and make arbitrary external calls in its own name; on the other hand, its only finality check is compared with the residual value stored in transient storage, neither clearing it to zero nor checking whether the claim was actually completed in this call. An attacker first writes the checksum with a genuine claim, then reuses that value with a second claim, causing the Arbitrator to call the gateway's `onlyArbitrator` interface on their behalf, ultimately writing the forged batch root into ZkLink, thus "proving" the asset within the bridge as retrievable. The fix should start from three levels. First, `claimMessage` must clear `finalizeMessageHash` before `Address.functionCall`, and after the call, it must be non-zero and equal to the current claim, or bound with an incrementing nonce for each call, ensuring that the checksum can only be written by `receiveMessage` in this call. Second, add a whitelist to `_sourceChainCanonicalMessageService` to prohibit gateways registered by the Arbitrator contract itself from being treated as "source chain message services"; at the same time, do not register dev auxiliary contracts as relayers, or at least add access controls for them to prevent arbitrary addresses from indirectly gaining the ability to call `claimMessage`. Third, `ZkLink.syncBatchRoot` should refuse to overwrite existing batch roots, and add independent proofs on the gateway side or message layer so that batch root updates cannot be effective solely based on "the caller being a gateway". The SlowMist security team recommends that when reviewing the code of similar cross-chain relay projects, it should focus on checking four points: whether transient storage is reset before each call, whether the checksum comes from the same source as the actual executed parameters, whether the "trusted caller" could be indirectly borrowed by any user (e.g., through a public helper or relayer), and whether independent verification is performed when updating the batch root. These kinds of problems are often not in the most obvious asset transfer functions, but in the middle layer of contracts that "appear to be just forwarding" assets.

data.title: After such a significant drop: Has the A-share market bottomed out?
data.description:
This month, stock market investors are likely to be in a bad mood. Various stock indices have plummeted, with the Shanghai Composite Index falling below 3600 points, and the ChiNext Index and STAR Market 50 Index both experiencing monthly declines of over 20%. Looking at a longer timeframe, the situation is even worse, with the ChiNext Index retreating 45% from its June high and the STAR Market 50 Index retreating 49% from its July high. The hardest-hit sectors are concentrated in the hottest sectors of the first half of the year. Especially in the computing power hardware sector, CPO and PCB sectors collectively collapsed, with many core leading stocks being halved in value, and some even experiencing maximum declines exceeding 70%, almost returning to or even lower than the starting point of the AI ​​narrative-driven rally in 2025. In contrast, food and beverage rose 5.31%, banking rose 4.84%, and oil and petrochemicals rose 3.34%, with dividend and defensive assets bucking the trend and reaching new highs. This extreme divergence of "growth collapse and value-driven capital attraction" is itself a typical signal that market sentiment has entered an extreme zone. Since it has fallen to an extreme level, does that mean that a temporary bottom is not far away? I. Valuation, Sentiment, Capital, and Policy: Multiple Indicators Entering Extreme Zones First, let's look at valuation. As of today's closing, the CSI 300's TTM P/E ratio is approximately 12.94, placing it at approximately the 55.5th percentile over the past ten years, while its P/B ratio is approximately 1.34, placing it at approximately the 26.89th percentile over the past ten years. The current valuation of the CSI 300 is about half that of the S&P 500 (24.71 times) and significantly lower than the Nikkei 225's 19 times. The ChiNext Index's TTM P/E ratio is approximately 27.2 times, only at the 4.1% percentile over the past ten years. Looking at the dynamic P/E ratio, the projected P/E ratios for 2026 and 2027 have decreased to 23 times and 16 times respectively, indicating that the valuation premium of growth stocks has been significantly digested. Secondly, look at sentiment and volatility indicators. Currently, the volatility of both the Shanghai Composite Index and the ChiNext Index has risen to a relatively high level, entering a period of extreme volatility. From the perspective of implied volatility of options, the panic sentiment of the ChiNext Index, CSI 1000, and STAR Market 50 is approaching the 90th percentile historically. Regarding trading congestion, the top 5% of stocks by trading volume accounted for approximately 40.9% of total trading volume as of October 23, a decrease of nearly 10 percentage points from the end of June, indicating a significant reduction in the congestion risk previously anticipated. Meanwhile, the overall sentiment index dropped to 17%, with only 23% of stocks trading above their 20-day moving average, further indicating that market sentiment has reached a low point. Thirdly, there's the issue of trading volume and liquidity. Looking back at the trading volume during this round of adjustments, the average daily turnover of A-shares has decreased from a peak of over 3 trillion yuan in June to approximately 1.6 trillion yuan since October, shrinking by nearly half. On October 27th, the total turnover of the two markets shrank to 1.47 trillion yuan, marking the 19th consecutive trading day below 2 trillion yuan. However, it is worth noting that on October 28th, there was a rebound with increased volume to 1.64 trillion yuan, and on October 30th, the final trading day, the total turnover of the two markets reached 1.67 trillion yuan. Especially today, the market saw a significant drop in trading volume, with a large decline in the index and many individual stocks falling. From a technical perspective, the possibility of a bottoming out cannot be ruled out. Regarding leveraged funds, the balance of margin trading and securities lending has fallen by nearly 20% from its peak, and the margin balance has shrunk by over 160 billion yuan for 13 consecutive days. The average collateral ratio has dropped to around 250%, approaching the level seen during the tariff impact in April 2025, indicating that the passive reduction of leveraged funds may be nearing its end. In the last week of October, stock ETFs continued to see significant net inflows, primarily from institutional ETFs. Northbound capital resumed net buying of A-shares, and actively managed equity funds slightly increased their positions. Meanwhile, margin trading continued to see net outflows of 57 billion yuan, reaching its lowest level since late September 2024. The divergence between passive deleveraging and active buying by allocation-oriented funds has historically corresponded to the tail end of panic selling rather than a continuation of a downtrend. There are also policy and fundamental factors at play. Recently, regulators have been making significantly more pronounced calls to stabilize the market. At the Financial Street Forum Annual Meeting on October 27, regulators explicitly emphasized "making every effort to safeguard the safety and stability of the capital market." The People's Bank of China simultaneously established a non-bank large-scale redemption swap facility in the bond market, aiming to break the negative feedback loop caused by redemptions of asset management products. Today, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) held a Party Committee meeting, emphasizing making every effort to stabilize the market and expectations, deepen comprehensive reforms in investment and financing, improve full-chain supervision, continuously enhance the resilience and confidence of the capital market, and ensure the successful completion of all tasks in the first year of the 15th Five-Year Plan. On the macroeconomic front, Q3 GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year, a 0.2 percentage point increase from Q2. Fixed asset investment ended its six-month decline in September, and retail sales growth rebounded. Profits of large-scale industrial enterprises grew by 15.5% from January to September. On the corporate front, several major technology companies recently released their Q3 financial reports, including CPO, PCB, and new energy companies. Even with high earnings growth, most of their stock prices fell, with some experiencing single-day drops exceeding 10%. This means that even if the original valuations were too high, the market is using the decline to forcefully squeeze out the valuation inflation. Through comprehensive comparison and cross-verification, the current A-share market possesses a mixed characteristic of valuation bottom, sentiment bottom, policy bottom, and capital bottom to some extent. II. Highly Similar to the Logic of the Deep Adjustment in Early 2024 The deep adjustment before January 2024 was triggered by the complete reversal of the prosperity of the new energy sector, coupled with the severe over-extension of valuations in the early stage. The ChiNext index retreated by more than 40% from its 2023 high, and the stock prices of most leading companies in the sector were halved. The current situation is similar. The STAR Market 50 and ChiNext indices have retreated nearly 30% from their year-to-date highs, while leading stocks in mainstream sectors such as AI computing power, semiconductors, and advanced manufacturing have generally retreated by over 40%. The severity of the individual stock declines is almost identical to the sector clearing in January 2024. This may be the recurring cycle for A-share growth stocks: consensus expectations drive up valuations → a turning point in the economic cycle appears → concentrated profit-taking and panic selling → a double whammy of valuation and performance declines. The script hasn't changed; only the sector name has changed from new energy to AI technology. In terms of capital flows, in January 2024, northbound capital continued to flow out and sell off core assets. The decline in public fund net asset value triggered redemptions, and institutions were forced to reduce their holdings of heavily weighted stocks. This was compounded by margin trading liquidations, quantitative strategies following suit, and concentrated buying by Xueqiu products. Under the combined pressure of multiple selling pressures, growth stocks lost their support, and the downward slope continued to widen. The current situation is similar. Capital is experiencing a continuous net outflow in stages, with leading growth stocks heavily held by institutions bearing the brunt. They can only passively reduce their holdings in the most liquid sectors, and low-level liquidations are constantly emerging. Coupled with the convergence of quantitative trading, selling pressure is concentrated during the decline, exacerbating the index's downward trend. Both rounds of market rallies were typical examples of zero-sum games. Without new funds to support the market, any concentrated sell-off would be amplified exponentially. Another perspective is the extreme structural divergence. In January 2024, while growth stocks continued to adjust, high-dividend sectors such as coal, utilities, and banks bucked the trend and even reached new highs. Funds withdrew from overvalued growth stocks and flowed into undervalued, high-certainty dividend assets, pushing style divergence to its extreme. And now? High-dividend defensive sectors such as banking, energy, and utilities have become a safe haven for existing funds: the market capitalization of the four major banks has exceeded 10 trillion yuan for the first time, and PetroChina has surged more than 64% since July, reaching a new high in 18 years. Historically, this extreme divergence in styles is often one of the signals of a temporary bottom. When existing funds flock to defensive sectors and the selling pressure in growth stocks is fully released, it means that the correction has entered its second half. Furthermore, the market's eventual bottoming out and reversal in January 2024 was primarily due to the confirmation of a policy bottom. Prior to that bottom, regulators issued frequent statements to stabilize expectations, Huijin continuously increased its ETF holdings to support liquidity, trading platforms tightened short-selling mechanisms, and expectations for monetary easing rose. This multi-dimensional policy synergy ultimately reversed the panic-driven expectation of a one-sided decline. The pace of the market-stabilizing policies was also similar. Recently, regulators have begun to express their commitment to continuously optimizing the market ecosystem, strictly regulating share reductions, tightening securities lending rules, and guiding medium- and long-term funds into the market. On the funding front, there has been an increase in listed companies' share buybacks and major shareholders' share increases, gradually signaling the entry of industrial capital. Of course, the transmission from the policy bottom to the market bottom takes time, and sentiment recovery will not happen overnight. The bottom is always the most agonizing stage, but it is also the window of opportunity for the most cost-effective long-term investment.

III. Policy bottom is not equal to market bottom; bottoming still needs time

Policy pronouncements can support the lower limit, but there are still some bearish factors. The bottoming process is unlikely to be a straight line, but rather a process of repeated grinding.

For example, domestically, many sectors of the macroeconomy still need time to recover or be boosted. This is the fundamental key to whether companies can earn more profits to support market capitalization growth.

At the market level, the high-priced shares of technology stocks may not have been fully cleared in the short term.

Currently, margin trading funds are still experiencing significant net outflows. Although institutional holdings in the previously heavily weighted telecommunications and electronics sectors have decreased somewhat, the innovation and entrepreneurship sector is simultaneously facing a slowdown in third-quarter earnings growth and the digestion of overcrowding, meaning it is under pressure from both "performance and shareholding." This clearing process usually takes time and cannot be completed with a single announcement. More importantly, influencing factors come from overseas. For example, the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again in December, and US Treasury yields are putting downward pressure on valuations. Amidst the escalating tensions in the Middle East, international oil prices have soared to over $100. High oil prices will make inflation more persistent, make it more difficult for the Federal Reserve to ease monetary policy, and directly suppress global risk appetite, forming a negative chain of "oil price—inflation—interest rate—valuation." The market's pricing in a December rate hike is still high, and the 10-year US Treasury yield is above 5%. As long as long-term interest rates do not trend downwards, the valuations of global growth stocks, especially the overvalued stocks on the A-share ChiNext and STAR Market, will remain suppressed. Furthermore, doubts about whether AI can "make money" continue to simmer. Especially in the last two days, as US tech giants entered their earnings season, some of the performance indicators or guidance disclosed by giants such as Google, Intel, and Amazon fell short of expectations, triggering sharp declines and causing the market to question whether AI investments can translate into profits. Against this backdrop, it will be difficult for A-shares to break out of their current pattern in the short term. After all, A-shares are closely tied to overseas AI giants in the computing power chain, and many core leading companies rely heavily on these giants for orders. The sentiment of these major investors will inevitably be transmitted, causing short-term volatility. In addition, another factor to watch out for is that the US-China technology friction could easily trigger a sudden market crash with seemingly minor announcements. This risk has already caused several pullbacks in A-share technology stocks recently, a tail-end disturbance that cannot be ignored during the bottoming-out period. Therefore, in general, the current market policy bottom provides the boundary for downside potential, but these negative domestic and international variables determine how long the bottoming-out process will take and how tortuous the path will be. Especially in the technology growth sector, overseas interest rates and the AI ​​narrative are the two lines that are most difficult to offset with domestic policies in the short term. However, what is certain is that the current A-share market has indeed reached a relatively low level, and it may not be far from a temporary bottom. For long-term funds, the cost-effectiveness at this level is improving; for short-term sentiment, it's likely that the bottoming process won't be immediate. This moment truly tests one's composure and strategic vision.
